stories.title: A Deepawali birth in Arvi
stories.summary: Dattopant Thengadi was born in Arvi, Wardha, Maharashtra, on Deepawali day, 10 November 1920.
stories.body:
Dattatreya Bapurao Thengadi — remembered by the world as Dattopant Thengadi — was born in the village of Arvi in the Wardha district of Maharashtra on the day of Deepawali, 10 November 1920.

He was born into a middle-class family. His father was Bapurao Dajiba Thengadi and his mother was Janaki Devi.

The boy from a small Maharashtra town would grow into one of the foremost organisation builders of modern India — a man who, over some six decades of public life, nurtured workers and institutions that still carry his thought forward.

stories.title: A leader at fifteen
stories.summary: At just fifteen, he was already leading the Vanar Sena and the student union of his high school in Arvi.
stories.body:
Leadership showed early in Thengadi Ji's life. At the age of fifteen he led the Vanar Sena, the children's wing associated with the freedom movement, and headed the student union of his municipal high school in Arvi.

These were small beginnings, but they point to a pattern that marked his whole career: a quiet capacity to gather people, give them a purpose and keep them organised.

stories.title: From Morris College to the law
stories.summary: He studied at Morris College and took an LLB at the Law College in Nagpur.
stories.body:
Thengadi Ji pursued higher studies at Morris College, Nagpur, and then took his law degree (LLB) from the Law College in Nagpur.

His legal training and his command of ideas — he was equally at home with Marxist theory and with the Indian tradition — later helped him argue for an indigenous labour movement on firm intellectual ground.

stories.title: 1942: a life given to the nation
stories.summary: In 1942 he became a full-time RSS pracharak, a commitment he kept until his death in 2004.
stories.body:
Impressed by the life and vision of Dr Keshav Baliram Hedgewar, the founder of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, Thengadi Ji decided to dedicate his life to the nation by becoming a Sangh pracharak in 1942.

He remained a full-time pracharak until his last day on 14 October 2004.

His early assignments took him across the country: Kerala from 1942 to 1944, Bengal from 1945 to 1947 and Assam in 1948–49 — a grounding in the diversity of Bharat that shaped his later organising work.

stories.title: Learning the tools of the trade
stories.summary: Before founding BMS he worked inside the existing labour organisations to learn how trade unions actually function.
stories.body:
When he turned to the labour field, Thengadi Ji did not begin by criticising from the outside. He worked within the existing labour organisations — among them INTUC, where he served as an organising secretary in 1950–51 — and was associated with unions of postal and railway workers.

He studied how trade unions function, what they achieved and where they fell short. Prof. Rakesh Sinha notes that he did this to learn the tools of trade unionism before building something new.

Entrusted with building a labour organisation, Thengadi Ji humbly admitted that he had no experience of it — and set about learning.

links.label: He changed the paradigm of the trade union movement — Prof. Rakesh Sinha

stories.title: Jana Sangh years and the Rajya Sabha
stories.summary: He served the Bharatiya Jana Sangh as an organiser and sat in the Rajya Sabha for two terms between 1964 and 1976.
stories.body:
In the early 1950s Thengadi Ji worked as organising secretary of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh in Madhya Pradesh, and later in South India.

He was elected to the Rajya Sabha from the Jana Sangh for two terms between 1964 and 1976, and served as its vice-chairman in 1968–70.

Even in Parliament he stayed what he had always been — a worker among workers, who used the platform to speak for labour, farmers and the common citizen.

stories.title: 23 July 1955: BMS is born
stories.summary: The Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh was founded on 23 July 1955 at Bhopal.
stories.body:
On 23 July 1955 Dattopant Thengadi founded the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh at Bhopal. The labour movement of the time was dominated by Left philosophy, and BMS began as a deliberate alternative rooted in national thought.

During discussions on what to call the new organisation, Thengadi Ji himself had suggested the name Shramjivi Sangathan. In the end the name Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh was chosen because it was simple and meaningful.

BMS started from scratch, and he spent decades patiently building it — a journey that made it, in time, the largest central trade union organisation in the country.

stories.title: The three-line motto
stories.summary: Nationalise the Labour, Labourise the Industry, Industrialise the Nation — the slogan that defines BMS.
stories.body:
When socialism and communism were the buzzwords of the day, Thengadi Ji's three-line motto was a bold and unconventional idea: **Nationalise the Labour, Labourise the Industry, Industrialise the Nation.**

*Nationalise the Labour* means to instil national feeling and pride in the worker. *Labourise the Industry* means that workers are co-owners of the industry once labour is fairly valued as capital. *Industrialise the Nation* means that the country's growth must come through sustainable industry.

Seven decades later, the motto is still printed on every BMS banner and publication.

stories.title: Workers unite the world
stories.summary: In 1955 the popular slogan was ‘Workers of the world, unite’. BMS answered with ‘Workers unite the world’.
stories.body:
In the 1950s the slogan raised by the dominant labour groups was ‘Workers of the world, unite!’. BMS saw in it a call for disruption and class hatred.

The answer was a slogan that turned the sentence around: **Workers unite the world.** The worker is not a destroyer but a builder, and labour is a force that can bring the divided world together.

The older cry of ‘Inquilab Zindabad’ at labour gatherings gradually made way for ‘Bharat Mata ki Jai’ — a change that tells the story of how Indian labour found its own voice.

stories.title: Rashtra hit, Udyog hit, Mazdoor hit
stories.summary: राष्ट्रहित · उद्योगहित · मजदूरहित: the interests of the nation, the industry and the worker must be protected together.
stories.body:
Thengadi Ji gave BMS a cyclic, holistic philosophy summed up in three words: **Rashtra Hita, Udyoga Hita, Mazdoor Hita** — the interest of the nation, of the industry and of the worker.

None of the three is to be sacrificed for another. A worker's welfare depends on a healthy industry, a healthy industry serves the nation, and the nation's strength rests on the dignity of its workers.

This is why BMS treats strikes as a last resort after talks, negotiation and arbitration: it does not oppose workers' demands, but insists they are pursued with the national interest in mind.

stories.title: Class cooperation, not class conflict
stories.summary: BMS replaced the idea of class struggle with cooperation among the stakeholders of production.
stories.body:
Thengadi Ji organised large-scale labour movements on the idea that class cooperation should take the place of class conflict.

The Marxist model sees capital and labour as eternal enemies. Thengadi Ji, drawing on the Indian tradition, saw them as partners in a common national task, whose differences are to be settled through dialogue.

Seventy years on, the BMS style — firm in demands, constructive in method — is a recognised part of India's labour relations.

links.label: He changed the paradigm of the trade union movement — Prof. Rakesh Sinha

stories.title: Labourisation: labour is also capital
stories.summary: Workers are co-owners of the industry once their labour is fairly valued as capital.
stories.body:
BMS promotes the idea of ‘labourisation’, founded on the theory that workers are co-owners of the industry if their labour capital is fairly valued.

This thinking echoes M. S. Golwalkar ‘Guruji’, who said at the 1973 Thane meeting that in every industry labour is also one form of capital.

Following from this, BMS calls for a national commission on industrial ownership, which should recommend a pattern of ownership for each industry according to its specific features and the needs of the national economy.

stories.title: Vishwakarma Jayanti: India's own Labour Day
stories.summary: BMS made Vishwakarma Jayanti, 17 September, the National Labour Day, in place of the imported May Day tradition.
stories.body:
BMS has argued that India's labour festival should come from India's own tradition. It established Vishwakarma Jayanti — 17 September — as National Labour Day, honouring Lord Vishwakarma, the divine craftsman, as the patron of all who work with their hands and skills.

BMS also coined the term ‘Vishwakarma sector’ for the vast self-employed, skilled workforce of artisans and craftspeople, who never fitted the Marxist category of employer and employee.

The BMS view-points section carries an article titled ‘Vishwakarma Jayanti versus May Day’ for those who want to read the argument.

stories.title: Overtaking the biggest union
stories.summary: Formed in 1955, BMS overtook INTUC to become the largest trade union in India in about three decades.
stories.body:
BMS began as the smallest of unions. Yet S. Gurumurthy recalls that within about three decades it overtook INTUC, then the largest trade union. By 1989 its strength was over 31 lakh.

Prof. Krishna Chandra Mishra writes that Thengadi Ji worked for 49 years to make it the world's largest trade union, proof that he was among the best organisers.

Today BMS represents India at the International Labour Organisation and other international forums.

stories.title: Standing against the Emergency
stories.summary: In 1975 he organised protests as part of the anti-Emergency movement.
stories.body:
When the Emergency was declared in 1975, Thengadi Ji organised protests as part of the anti-Emergency movement.

He was not a man to keep silent on matters that affected the life of the nation. He used his organisational network, and his years in public life, to help the movement for the restoration of democracy.

stories.title: A founder of the student movement
stories.summary: He helped set up the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad in 1949.
stories.body:
Thengadi Ji was a founder-member of the Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP), set up in 1949, the student organisation that went on to become one of the largest in the country.

It was typical of him: he planted the seeds of institutions in many fields, and then stepped back to let others lead them.

stories.title: Bharatiya Kisan Sangh, 1979
stories.summary: He founded the Bharatiya Kisan Sangh on 4 March 1979, building the largest union of agriculturists.
stories.body:
After labour, Thengadi Ji turned to the farmer. He formed the Bharatiya Kisan Sangh on 4 March 1979.

He was a trade union leader, but not an ‘urbanite’; and not a ‘village versus town’ man. S. Gurumurthy notes that he built the country's largest union of farmers while seeing agriculture and industry as partners.

links.label: A great void difficult to fill

stories.title: Ambedkar and the Samajik Samarasata Manch
stories.summary: He was close to Dr B. R. Ambedkar and founded the Samajik Samarasata Manch on 14 April 1983.
stories.body:
Thengadi Ji could speak about Babasaheb Ambedkar with authority, because he was closely with him during the last years of Ambedkar's life.

On 14 April 1983, Ambedkar Jayanti, he formed the Samajik Samarasata Manch, a platform for social harmony.

He also wrote about Ambedkar — a book on Dr Babasaheb Ambedkar by him was released in Bhopal in October 2005 by RSS Sarsanghachalak K. S. Sudarshan.

links.label: A great void difficult to fill

stories.title: Swadeshi Jagaran Manch, 1991
stories.summary: On 22 November 1991 he formed the Swadeshi Jagaran Manch to articulate an indigenous economic model.
stories.body:
With liberalisation and the emergence of the WTO, Thengadi Ji saw the need to raise the awareness of the people of developing countries about multinational corporations and Western economic interests.

He formed the Swadeshi Jagaran Manch on 22 November 1991. As S. Gurumurthy puts it, it articulated an alternative indigenous economic model, not just opposition to globalisation.

stories.title: Paryavaran, Sarva Panth Samadar and more
stories.summary: He also founded the Paryavaran Manch and the Sarva Panth Samadar Manch.
stories.body:
Alongside the larger bodies, Thengadi Ji founded or nurtured the Paryavaran Manch (environment) and the Sarva Panth Samadar Manch, which works for equal respect among all faiths.

He was also associated with Sanskar Bharati, the Swadeshi Science Movement, the Bharatiya Vichar Kendra and the Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat for consumers.

stories.title: A lawyers' forum and a consumer voice
stories.summary: He co-founded the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad and the Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat.
stories.body:
Thengadi Ji, a law graduate himself, was closely associated with the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad, the national lawyers' council, and the Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat, which speaks for consumers.

His book *Consumer: A Sovereign without Sovereignty* captures his concern for the ordinary buyer in the market.

stories.title: The books he wrote
stories.summary: Third Way, Modernization without Westernization, Why Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh?, Our National Renaissance and more.
stories.body:
Thengadi Ji was a prolific thinker. Among his books are *The Third Way*, *Modernization without Westernization*, *Why Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh?*, *Consumer: A Sovereign without Sovereignty*, *Spectrum*, *Our National Renaissance*, *The Perspective*, *Global Economic System: A Hindu View* and *Marx and Deen Dayal: Two Approaches*.

Together they set out a Bharatiya alternative to both capitalism and communism, and a vision of modernisation without Westernisation.

stories.title: Swadeshi economics and the ‘third way’
stories.summary: He argued for an indigenous economic path that is neither capitalist nor communist.
stories.body:
Thengadi Ji is regarded as one of the foremost ideologues of Swadeshi economics. In his writing he presented the Hindu way of economics, technology, environment and legal systems as a coherent alternative.

His ‘third way’ rejects the exploitative nature of capitalism and the class struggle of communism. In recent years many have seen in it the early roots of the idea of Atmanirbhar Bharat.

links.label: The Organiser: A man neither after power nor post

stories.title: A voice beyond India's borders
stories.summary: As founder-president of BMS he travelled to many countries to present the Indian view on labour.
stories.body:
As the founder-president of the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh, Thengadi Ji travelled abroad on labour and organisational work — to Russia, Hungary, Geneva, the USA, Canada and other countries.

The life profile published by the V.V. Giri National Labour Institute also notes a message of his that was broadcast by Beijing Radio on 28 April 1985.

Everywhere he carried the same message: that the Indian worker has a distinct national vision and a voice of his own.

stories.title: A man neither after power nor post
stories.summary: He turned down the Padma Bhushan and never sought office for himself.
stories.body:
Those who knew him describe a man who never looked for recognition. He was awarded the Padma Bhushan, but he declined to accept it.

S. Gurumurthy wrote that the creator of the BMS, the Kisan Sangh and the SJM was himself not widely known — a *tapasvi* who worked for the nation and stayed in the background.

stories.title: 14 October 2004 — and his legacy
stories.summary: He passed away at Pune on 14 October 2004. His work and name live on.
stories.body:
Dattopant Thengadi passed away on 14 October 2004 at Pune, at the age of 83.

His legacy is the organisations he built, the thinkers he mentored and the workers who carry the saffron flag with the cry of ‘Bharat Mata ki Jai’. The BMS head office in New Delhi is named Dattopant Thengadi Bhawan, and the Central Board for Workers' Education under the Labour Ministry now carries his name as the Dattopant Thengadi National Board of Workers' Education and Development.

This was the last of the weekly stories. After it, the series begins again from the first.
